title: How a round goes
intro: Jiu-jitsu is unreadable as a list of moves and obvious as a map. Every position below is somewhere you can end up, stacked by what it is worth from your side: the best at the top, the worst at the bottom. The whole sport is trading upward — and when you lose ground, the way back is always the same three moves in the same order: survive, escape, recover.

bands.label: You are ahead
bands.note: Every one of these is worth more than the one below it, and the higher you are the fewer answers they have. Stabilise before you attack — reaching down for a submission is how you trade back down.

bands.label: Even
bands.note: Nobody is on top yet. Standing and the guards live together here on purpose: having someone in your guard is not losing, and it is not winning either. This band is where most of a round is actually spent.

bands.label: You are behind
bands.note: Bad, worse, worst — in that order going down. The way back is always the same three moves in the same order: survive, escape, recover. Panicking skips the first one, which is why it never works.

nodes.label: Their back
nodes.note: The best place in the sport, and the only one they cannot see. Chest to their back, both hooks or a body triangle, and their neck already yours.

nodes.label: Mount
nodes.note: Sitting on them with both legs outside. Stabilise before you attack: reaching for a submission from an unsettled mount is how you end up back in their guard.

nodes.label: North–south
nodes.note: Head to head, chest on their chest. A pin they cannot frame against the same way, and the place side control goes when they turn in.

nodes.label: Knee on belly
nodes.note: Mobile, heavy and worth points. It is a place you pass through on the way to mount, not one you settle in — and the library knows it as a detail of side control rather than a position of its own, which is why there are far fewer techniques here than next door.

nodes.label: Side control
nodes.note: Where a finished pass lands. Crossface and underhook first: a pass is not finished until the pin is, and everything above this position is reached from here.

nodes.label: On their turtle
nodes.note: They are balled up and you are on them. Seatbelt and go: turtle is a door, and the room on the other side of it is their back.

nodes.label: Inside their guard
nodes.note: On top, but their legs are still between you and them. Nothing above this is available until you pass, which is why passing is the whole job here. It opens the OPEN guard entry, because by the time you are working on top the closed guard has usually already been opened.

nodes.label: Half guard, on top
nodes.note: One leg trapped, and the underhook decides it. Half guard is not most of a pass — it is its own fight, and the winner of the underhook usually wins it.

nodes.label: Standing
nodes.note: Where every round starts and nobody is winning yet. Two exits that are not a takedown: pull guard on your terms, or disengage and reset.

nodes.label: Leg entanglement
nodes.note: Legs tangled, and neither of you is on top. A position with its own controls and its own escapes — treat it as one, not as a lottery.

nodes.label: Your guard
nodes.note: Underneath, with your legs between you and them. The only bottom position that attacks: sweep them, submit them, or come up to your feet. It opens the CLOSED guard entry, because that is the guard you are taught first and the one you will play most on the bottom.

nodes.label: Half guard, on the bottom
nodes.note: One of their legs trapped between yours. Not a guard that half-failed — a real position, and the underhook is what it is fought over.

nodes.label: Turtled
nodes.note: On your knees, balled up. Somewhere you move through, never somewhere you wait: staying still here is volunteering your back.

nodes.label: Under side control
nodes.note: Pinned across the chest. Uncomfortable rather than dangerous, and you can keep it that way — frames first, then move your hips, then recover.

nodes.label: Under mount
nodes.note: The worst place a beginner spends time. Elbows to knees, and get out before they climb: high mount is much harder to escape than low.

nodes.label: Back taken
nodes.note: The worst place in the sport. Two hands to your neck first, then get your shoulders to the floor and turn in — in that order, every time.

edges.label: They take you down and pass
